idiom_name: value-type views: the owning view (or an @Observable model) is the supply half; subviews take plain values or @Binding
implementation_notes: SwiftUI makes the presentational half the natural shape: a View is a value, so a subview that receives its input as a plain property cannot mutate it, and the type system enforces the direction of the data flow. The supply half is the view that owns the model - @State for view-lifetime values, an @Observable model (or @StateObject / @ObservedObject on older standards) for data that outlives the view - and it passes values down, plus a @Binding where a child must write back. What replaces the classic container component is the framework's dependency tracking: a view re-renders when the observable property its body read changes, so no wrapper is needed to hand data down. The UIKit variant below remains for imperative view hierarchies.
pitfalls: SwiftUI views are transient values: never cache a view or share it between controllers, and never expect a subview to keep its own copy of the data.
@State mirrors the view's lifetime and disappears with it; data that must survive navigation or relaunch belongs in an observable model or a store.
Reading an observable property outside body (for example inside an escaping closure) does not register the dependency, so the view will not update when it changes.

variants.name: UIKit: view controller as supply half, passive views
variants.idiom_name: UIViewController owning data and view hierarchy; UIView children configured only through setters
variants.implementation_notes: In UIKit the view controller is the supply half: it owns the data, loads it asynchronously and configures its view hierarchy, and it is documented as the sole owner of those views, so child views stay passive displays that never fetch anything themselves. Cross-controller navigation repeats the split one level up through container view controllers (addChild / removeFromParent), and MVVM is the refinement where a view-model object holds the data while the controller only binds it. Prefer this variant in existing UIKit applications or where imperative control over the view hierarchy is required.
pitfalls: Retain cycles: a closure that captures the controller strongly while the controller owns the closure; capture self weakly.
Updating views from a background thread corrupts layout; marshal state changes onto the main actor or main queue.
A controller that reads the model once in viewDidLoad renders a single snapshot; subscribe to changes in the supply half instead.
